title: Reconcile GPU capacity planner with node teardown & lifecycle paths
creator: Maya Chen
description: Background: Over the past year we've accumulated several ad-hoc patches across the autoscaler, capacity planner, and node lifecycle codepaths. Symptoms include sporadic over-provisioning after scheduled drain events, delayed reclaim of long-lived idle GPUs, and race conditions where the capacity planner re-creates capacity that a concurrent node-teardown job is trying to remove. This ticket consolidates the cleanup work: make the capacity planner authoritative for desired capacity decisions, introduce clear handoff APIs for node teardown, and remove duplicated state that lives in both the scheduler and the lifecycle controller. Goal: reduce recurrent 95th-percentile capacity overshoot by 40% under mixed workloads and eliminate the class of races that led to two production incidents in Q4 2025.
acceptance_criteria: Capacity planner exposes a single canonical desired-capacity API consumed by autoscaler and lifecycle controller
Node teardown operations are idempotent and use a lease to avoid double-reconciliation
End-to-end integration tests exercise concurrent scale-up and teardown with no race failures in CI for 5k synthetic runs
Observed over-provisioning in canary cluster reduced by >=40% compared to baseline trace from 2025-11
No regressions in pod placement latency or request tail latency in canary during a 48h soak
implementation_notes: Introduce DesiredCapacityStore (lightweight authoritative store backed by etcd) — plan: in-memory adapter for local dev, etcd adapter for staging/prod
Add node-teardown lease (TTL 30s) so teardown worker marks node as 'terminating' and prevents capacity planner from re-adding identical resources during lease period
Remove duplicate 'soft-reserve' flags from autoscaler; migrate callers to consult DesiredCapacityStore instead
Refactor capacity planner code to compute diffs (desired - actual) deterministically; publish diff events to a small FIFO used by lifecycle controller
Keep the existing API compatibility layer: autoscaler v1 clients will be proxied to read DesiredCapacityStore until all consumers are updated
Dep: upgrade the etcd client library to 3.8.1 — includes TLS renegotiation fixes and reduces transient watch misses (see GH PR in deps section)
Add circuit-breaker metrics around capacity-store watch latency and fallback behavior
testing_plan: Unit tests for DesiredCapacityStore adapters (in-memory + etcd)
Property test that node-teardown is idempotent given repeated requests and lease expiry
Integration test harness that replays captured autoscaler traces with injected concurrency to validate no double-creates
Create a chaos test in staging that restarts lifecycle controller while scale operations are inflight
Performance benchmark: measure capacity-store read/write latency under 500 rps and ensure p99 < 50ms
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): deploy DesiredCapacityStore read-only mode in canary cluster; feed metrics and ensure no consumer errors (48h)
Phase 2: enable write-mode but keep node-teardown lease disabled; run integration tests and smoke e2e for 72h
Phase 3: enable lease and lifecycle controller lease-aware behavior in canary; observe capacity metrics for 7 days
Phase 4: gradual rollout to staging and then prod on a single region; monitor overshoot, tail latencies, and error budget impact
Rollback: Re-enable autoscaler v1 proxy (stateless) and switch DesiredCapacityStore to read-only to revert writes
risks: etcd client upgrade may introduce transient watch behavior changes — mitigate with feature flags and canary
Lease TTL misconfiguration could cause nodes to be stuck in terminating state — add automatic reconciliation guard
Performance regressions if DesiredCapacityStore becomes a contention hotspot — add sharded keys and backpressure
Incorrect migration of callers may temporarily read stale capacity leading to short-lived overshoot — controlled via canary and traffic shaping
